strengths: Addresses a genuine gap: existing LLM memory benchmarks (LoCoMo, LongMemEval, DialSim, etc.) focus on static long-input reading comprehension, while MemoryBench targets continual learning from user feedback and procedural memory, which is a well-motivated and under-explored evaluation setting.

Provides a clear and well-grounded taxonomy (declarative vs. procedural memory; explicit vs. implicit, verbose vs. action feedback) drawn from cognitive science and IR literature, and uses it to position MemoryBench against prior benchmarks in Table 1.

The benchmark is broad and heterogeneous: 11 public datasets across open/legal/academic domains, English and Chinese, and four input/output length regimes (LiSo/SiLo/LiLo/SiSo), with unified case format (q, v, c) and per-dataset native metrics.

The feedback simulation design is thoughtful and documented in detail: a hybrid of metric-derived satisfaction for verifiable tasks and LLM-as-user for open-ended tasks, plus a probabilistic action model calibrated to empirical user-behavior statistics (Shuster et al., 2022; Chatterji et al., 2025), with prompts, hyperparameters, and conditional probability tables provided in the appendix.

Useful empirical findings beyond the benchmark itself: SOTA memory systems (A-Mem, Mem0, MemoryOS) fail to consistently beat naive RAG baselines on heterogeneous tasks (contradicting results reported only on LoCoMo), and a detailed efficiency analysis reveals severe, previously unreported memorization-time pathologies (e.g., Mem0's per-entry slowdown exceeding 20 minutes on DialSim-theoffice).

Good reproducibility posture: data processing scripts, user simulators, evaluation pipelines, baselines, and released feedback logs for off-policy learning are stated as open-sourced; the appendix is unusually thorough (per-dataset preparation, judge prompts, LoRA/SFT configurations, GPU setup).
weaknesses: The central construct—simulated user feedback—is only weakly validated. The LLM-as-user simulator (Qwen-32B) replaces real user behavior, and validation (A.3.5) merely shows that feeding back the same session's dialog improves the answer to the same question; there is no human study, no calibration against real user logs, and no analysis of whether simulated verbose feedback is realistic or systematically biased. Since the paper's premise is that benchmarks should test learning from feedback, the validity of this proxy is the key soundness question.

Evaluation depends heavily on LLM-as-judge (gpt-4o-mini for most datasets, plus judge-based metric merging for JuDGE, IdeaBench, SciTechNews), with no reported human-agreement analysis for the merged 1–10 scores. This introduces potential circularity and unknown bias in the headline rankings.

The score aggregation is ad hoc and potentially unstable: min-max normalization and z-scores computed across the tested systems make a system's score depend on which other baselines happen to be run, and merging heterogeneous metrics (e.g., readability indices and ROUGE in SciTechNews) via a single judge prompt loses information without justification.

Internal inconsistencies undermine confidence in the results: Crime F1 is 0.0000 for all systems in Table 9 but 0.95+ in Table 11; the text claims 'LLMsys with memory support mostly outperformed Vanilla' while Table 8 z-scores show Vanilla competitive or best on many partitions; Table 2 lists 11 datasets but JRE-L appears only in later tables; Table 1 reports Kim et al. as 3121k cases. These suggest insufficient quality control over the data pipeline and reporting.

Statistical rigor is thin: only ~250 samples per dataset with a 4:1 split, no confidence intervals, significance tests, or variance estimates anywhere, despite many small between-system differences being interpreted as findings.

Baseline scope is limited: all conclusions rest on one backbone (Qwen3-8B, with a limited Qwen3-32B check), and on-policy results are reported only for fast systems (BM25/Embed), while the headline SOTA memory systems are excluded from the on-policy setting that most directly tests continual learning. The mapping choices for feeding feedback to each memory system (session vs. message) could also confound comparisons.

Polish issues: the reproducibility statement contains placeholder text ('open-sourced in and') with missing repository links; there are recurring typos, a broken citation (Wang et al., missing year), and hard-to-read results in the radial Figure 2, which carries the paper's main results.

The framing wavers between contributions: the abstract/introduction present MemoryBench as enabling continual learning evaluation, yet the main experimental findings show that existing systems largely fail to exploit feedback (with Vanilla beating all memory systems on SiLo), leaving the benchmark's discriminating power for actual continual learning (e.g., parametric adaptation beyond a small SFT/LoRA check) underexplored.

strengths: The problem is well-motivated and the identified gap is real: existing LLM memory benchmarks (LoCoMo, DialSim, LongMemEval, etc.) largely test static reading comprehension over long contexts, whereas MemoryBench explicitly targets procedural memory and learning from user feedback accumulated at service time. This is a meaningful and underexplored angle.

The taxonomy (declarative/procedural memory; explicit/implicit feedback) is clearly articulated and grounded in prior neuroscience and IR literature (Sections 2.1, Table 1), and the comparative positioning of existing benchmarks in Table 1 is useful for the community.

The evaluation is unusually thorough in scope: 11 underlying datasets across 3 domains, 2 languages, and 4 input/output length regimes; both off-policy and on-policy settings; multiple feedback types (verbose text, like/dislike, copy); plus an efficiency analysis (Fig. 3, Table 14) that few benchmarks report.

The finding that SOTA memory systems (A-Mem, Mem0, MemoryOS) fail to consistently beat naive RAG baselines outside narrow LoCoMo-style settings, and that feedback logs can add noise, is a valuable negative result with careful diagnosis (Section 3.3, Appendix A.3).

Reproducibility effort is substantial: data processing scripts, simulators, baselines, and pre-generated off-policy feedback logs are open-sourced, and the appendix provides detailed prompts, probabilistic action models, and hyperparameters.
weaknesses: Circularity and generality concerns from using the Qwen family for nearly everything: Qwen3-8B/32B as the backbone, Qwen3-32B as the user simulator, and gpt-4o-mini or Qwen-based critics as judges. The benchmark's headline conclusions (feedback quality, relative rankings) may be artifacts of a single model family's calibration; no independent simulator/judge agreement study with human validation is provided.

The simulated 'implicit feedback' is largely synthetic and derived deterministically from ground-truth metrics (e.g., DialSim S=3/S=9 mapping, Locomo F1-to-satisfaction thresholds, copy probability as 4x like probability). This calls into question whether the benchmark actually tests learning from realistic, noisy user behavior, or from a transparent oracle that trivially encodes the evaluation signal.

Metric aggregation is fragile: merging heterogeneous metrics via LLM-as-judge into a 1-10 score, then min-max normalization or z-scores pooled across datasets, is error-prone and makes the headline Figure 2 numbers hard to interpret. No reliability analysis (e.g., judge consistency, correlation with per-dataset metrics) is reported.

No statistical significance testing or variance reporting. Test sets are small (up to 250 samples per dataset, some as few as 25 in Table 6), and gains like those in Table 11 (e.g., +0.0036 METEOR, +0.0110 ROUGE-L) are well within plausible noise, yet are cited as evidence that simulated feedback is useful.

Evidence for the central claim that the benchmark enables 'continual learning' evaluation is thin: the on-policy results (Figs. 4-6) show fluctuating, non-monotonic curves without confidence intervals, and the tested memory systems were never designed for parametric continual learning, so the negative findings are somewhat expected rather than surprising.

Notable data/reporting inconsistencies undermine confidence: 'Crime F1' and 'Penalcode Index F1' are reported as 0.0000 for all systems in Table 9 despite non-zero recall/precision in the same table; DialSim #Case is listed as '3121k' in Table 1; the abstract-level claim of '20k' cases vs. the much smaller sampled testbeds in Tables 5-6 is not reconciled.

Several strong, relevant baselines are missing: full long-context baselines for the long-input tasks, other backbone families (e.g., Llama, GPT-class models), and at least one genuine parametric continual learning method, which limits what conclusions can be drawn about the 'continual learning' dimension the paper advertises.

Presentation issues: Figure 2 is nearly unreadable (tiny rotated labels, no clear ranking), Table 1's column alignment is confusing, and references contain incomplete entries (e.g., 'Wang et al.' with no year, an incomplete arXiv survey citation), suggesting the manuscript was not carefully proofread.

strengths: The paper addresses a genuine and clearly articulated gap: existing LLM memory benchmarks (LoCoMo, DialSim, LongMemEval-style) largely test static long-context reading comprehension, whereas MemoryBench targets procedural memory and continual learning from simulated user feedback at service time.

The taxonomy of memory (declarative/procedural, semantic/episodic) and feedback (explicit/implicit, verbose/action) is well motivated by neuroscience and IR literature (Atkinson & Shiffrin; Shen & Zhai), and Table 1 situates the contribution against prior benchmarks in a useful way.

The benchmark is broad: 11 public datasets spanning 3 domains, 2 languages, and 4 task-format partitions (LiSo/SiLo/LiLo/SiSo), with heterogeneous input/output lengths. The unified (q, v, c) case format is sensible.

The feedback simulation is thoughtfully engineered: a dual-path architecture (deterministic metric mapping for verifiable tasks; LLM-as-user with personas for open-ended tasks), plus a probabilistic action model (like/dislike/copy) calibrated to published user-behavior statistics (Shuster et al. 2022; Chatterji et al. 2025). Hyperparameters are documented and tunable.

Experimental coverage is substantial: off-policy and on-policy settings, two backbone sizes, time-consumption analysis, action-feedback and SFT variants, and stepwise training curves in the appendix. The appendix (prompts, sampling, per-dataset results) is unusually complete and supports reproducibility.

The headline negative finding — that SOTA memory systems (A-Mem, Mem0, MemoryOS) fail to consistently beat naive RAG baselines and are often slower — is valuable, and the authors honestly reconcile it with prior positive results by identifying design differences (generalization beyond LoCoMo-like tasks; failure to separate task context from feedback logs).

Data, preprocessing scripts, simulated feedback logs, and baseline implementations are open-sourced, and the ethics/reproducibility statements are present and appropriate for a benchmark built only on public data with simulated feedback.
weaknesses: Validity of the LLM-as-user feedback simulation is under-validated. The 'reasonable quality' claim rests mainly on with/without-feedback comparisons (Tables 11–12), where the same LLM family both generates and consumes feedback — a partially circular setup. No human study or correlation analysis of simulated verbose/action feedback against real user behavior is provided, even though the framework's central premise is that such feedback is a useful procedural-memory signal.

There appear to be metric-computation errors in the results. In Table 9 (JuDGE), Crime F1 and Penalcode Index F1 are reported as 0.0000 for all systems while the corresponding recall and precision are ~0.9–1.0, which is arithmetically impossible; Table 11 reports Crime F1 ≈ 0.955 for comparable settings. This undermines confidence in the per-dataset numbers underlying the aggregate scores.

The cross-dataset aggregation methodology is fragile. Merging heterogeneous metrics (ROUGE-L, F1, LLM-as-judge 1–10 scores, readability indices) via min-max normalization or z-scores, with LLM-as-judge used both for scoring and metric fusion, introduces substantial noise that is not quantified (no variance, confidence intervals, or significance tests are reported anywhere).

Findings that memory systems underperform RAG may partly be artifacts of configuration choices rather than intrinsic limitations — e.g., Mem0 is fed each full dialogue as a single memory entry, contexts are truncated for long inputs, Mem0 is excluded from Open-domain/LiSo, and the default retrieval count is five. The paper acknowledges the context/log-separation issue but the baseline configurations could bias the central 'SOTA memory systems are insufficient' claim.

Only one training session per case and a single fixed random seed are used in the off-policy setting; the on-policy/stepwise curves (Figs. 4–9) are erratic, and the paper interprets fluctuation as evidence that 'existing methods cannot filter feedback,' without ruling out sampling variance or judge noise as causes.

Several presentation issues: typos throughout ('lays in', 'isn't a well-developed benchmark', inconsistent 'Qwen-32B' vs 'Qwen3-32B'), the reproducibility statement contains broken link placeholders, the 3121k case count in Table 1 appears to be a formatting error, and Table 14 labels time in 'it/s' while Figure 3 states seconds, which is confusing.

The gap between the simulated-feedback regime and real deployment is acknowledged but not measured; given that commercial feedback logs differ in distribution from LLM-simulated ones, the practical import of benchmark rankings for continual learning research remains uncertain.

strengths: Addresses a genuine gap: existing LLM memory benchmarks are largely static reading-comprehension tests, whereas MemoryBench explicitly targets continual learning from accumulated user feedback (procedural memory), which is a well-motivated and underexplored evaluation axis (Sections 1, 2.1, Table 1).

Comprehensive and well-organized resource: 11 public datasets spanning 3 domains, 2 languages, and 4 input/output length regimes (~20k cases), with a clear taxonomy (declarative/procedural memory, explicit/implicit feedback) and unified task format (q, v, c).

Thorough experimental protocol: 8 baselines including SOTA memory systems (A-Mem, Mem0, MemoryOS), on-policy and off-policy settings, feedback-effect ablations (Tables 16-18), noisy-feedback robustness studies (A.3.9), backbone and simulator ablations (Table 22), and detailed time/latency analysis (Table 19, Fig. 4, A.3.8).

Honest and informative negative findings: SOTA memory systems fail to consistently outperform naive RAG, with a careful diagnosis of why this contradicts prior reports (Sec. 3.3), plus candid documentation of pathological behavior (e.g., Mem0's memorization slowdown, Fig. 11) and limitations discussion.

Validation of the user simulator via human annotation (A.2.5), probabilistic action modeling grounded in empirical user-behavior studies, and full open-sourcing of data, scripts, baselines, and feedback logs with explicit reproducibility and ethics statements.
weaknesses: Ecological validity of the central contribution rests entirely on LLM-simulated feedback. The human study (A.2.5) only shows annotators cannot distinguish simulated from human-written verbose feedback (with low kappa, 0.093 for naturalness); it does not establish that simulated feedback matches real user behavior distributions or that conclusions drawn from simulated feedback transfer to real service-time feedback. This is a significant caveat for the headline claims.

Potential circularity and bias in evaluation: the user simulator (Qwen3-32B) and the backbone (Qwen3-8B/32B) share a model family, and the LLM-as-judge aggregation (DeepSeek-V3, Qwen-based critic models) merges heterogeneous metrics into a single 1-10 score without reporting judge-human correlation for the aggregated score, adding evaluation noise to already noisy generative metrics.

Baseline configuration choices may disadvantage memory systems: e.g., Mem0 stores each full dialogue as a single memory entry, MemoryOS needed internal prompts translated, and contexts are truncated to fit input limits (Sec. 3.1, A.3.2). Some of the 'memory systems underperform RAG' conclusion may partly reflect suboptimal adaptation of these systems to heterogeneous tasks rather than a fundamental limitation, though the authors partially acknowledge this.

Small and uneven test sets (up to 250 samples per dataset, some subsets as small as 82-167 cases) with very large variance on several metrics (e.g., DialSim accuracy ±0.4-0.5, Table 13) make some per-dataset comparisons statistically fragile; no significance testing is reported.

Presentation issues reduce clarity: the main results are presented in a cluttered sunburst figure (Fig. 3) that is hard to read, with the corresponding numbers relegated to appendix tables; there are numerous typos and editing errors ('simlar', 'ouput', 'baselinefee', 'This This'), and the heavily skewed satisfaction-score distribution (Table 4: ~84% of scores are 8-9) limits the informativeness of the feedback signal, which is not analyzed.

The main reported setting (off-policy, verbose explicit feedback only) is a simplification; on-policy results are only available for a subset of systems due to runtime constraints, so the strongest claims about continual learning in deployment-like conditions are the least directly evidenced.

strengths: The paper targets a genuine gap: existing LLM memory benchmarks (LoCoMo, LongMemEval, MemBench, etc.) mostly test static reading comprehension over long contexts, whereas this work proposes evaluating continual improvement from simulated user feedback (procedural memory), which is a practically relevant and under-explored angle.

The benchmark aggregates a broad and heterogeneous collection of 11 public datasets across domains, languages, and input/output length regimes (LiSo/SiLo/LiLo/SiSo), plus both explicit (verbose, like/dislike) and implicit (copy, session exit) feedback types, providing reasonable coverage breadth.

The authors provide substantial infrastructure detail: feedback simulation prompts, probabilistic action models grounded in prior behavioral studies (Shuster et al., 2022; Chatterji et al., 2025), on-policy and off-policy protocols, efficiency analysis, noise-robustness studies, and released code/data/scripts for reproducibility.

The paper reports honest negative findings, e.g., that SOTA memory systems (A-Mem, Mem0, MemoryOS) do not consistently beat naive RAG baselines, and documents pathological inefficiencies (Mem0's superlinear memorization slowdown), which is useful diagnostic information for the community.
A human annotation study (200 cases, 9 annotators) is included to validate the fidelity of the simulated feedback.
weaknesses: Benchmark validity rests heavily on an LLM-as-user paradigm (Qwen3-32B), yet the validation is thin. The simulated satisfaction distribution in Table 4 is highly skewed and non-monotonic (41% of scores are 9, but only 0.43% are 10), which is hard to reconcile with the claimed 'reasonably good quality'; the human study has low Fleiss' Kappa on the key dimension (Naturalness 0.093) and only moderate win-rates (59%) on 200 samples, which does not convincingly support the claim that simulated feedback is 'indistinguishable from real human feedback'.

Circularity and judge-dependence: the same family of strong LLMs acts as user simulator, satisfaction scorer, metric merger (LLM-as-judge), and in several datasets (HelloBench, WritingBench, IdeaBench, NF-Cats) as the primary test metric. Since the memory systems being evaluated are also LLM-prompting pipelines, aggregate scores may largely reflect LLM-judge biases rather than memory/continual-learning ability. The min-max/z-score merging of heterogeneous metrics into a single 1-10 score further obscures interpretability, and no correlation study between the merged score and human judgment is provided.

The central negative claim — that SOTA memory systems underperform naive RAG — is confounded by weak baseline treatment: memory systems are run with default settings on datasets they were not designed for (e.g., A-Mem forced to use all-MiniLM-L6-v2 embeddings, context simply truncated to fit limits, retrieval count fixed at 5), while the authors themselves acknowledge prior systems used task-tailored chunking/summarization. The conclusion that 'generalizability is limited' may partly reflect an unfairly configured comparison rather than a property of the methods, and the sampled test sets are very small for some datasets (82, 167, 201 cases), so per-dataset differences may be noise.

The 'continual learning' framing overstates what is evaluated: the main results are essentially off-policy RAG over pre-generated feedback logs with a single Qwen3-8B backbone; no parametric continual learning method is evaluated in the main text (SFT appears only in an appendix with tiny filtered datasets), and no adaptation/RLHF-style method is included, so the benchmark's usefulness for its stated purpose (guiding continual-learning algorithm design) is not demonstrated.

Novelty claims are over-stated. The paper claims to be 'the first benchmark that can evaluate the continual learning ability of LLMsys on user feedback logs', but MemBench (Tan et al., 2025), MemSim (Zhang et al., 2024), and dialogue-simulation frameworks already cover substantial parts of this space; Table 1's dichotomy (all prior work lacks procedural/explicit/implicit feedback) is somewhat self-serving given these prior systems simulate interactions.

Missing or odd results undermine confidence: Mem0 and MemoryOS show large degradation on several datasets (e.g., MemoryOS accuracy 0.0000 on DialSim-theoffice, LimitGen-Syn accuracy 0.12 vs ~0.46 for everything else) that are explained only anecdotally; Mem0's pathological 6-12 hour memorization failure may be an integration artifact rather than an inherent property; the DialSim/LoCoMo path uses only binary deterministic feedback, so these datasets contribute little to the feedback-utilization story.

Writing and presentation quality is below the bar: frequent grammatical errors ('independent to tasks', 'a baselinfee', 'This This indicates', 'require significant engineering efforts'), Figure 3 (the headline results figure) is an unreadable radial chart with overlapping labels, and key setup decisions (e.g., how many sessions Vanilla receives, how feedback logs are formatted per system) are scattered across the appendix, hurting reproducibility of the headline comparison despite the reproducibility statement.

No statistical significance testing or seed variance for the main comparisons; given small test sets and LLM-judge variance, many of the observed rank orderings in Figure 3/Tables 10-11 (differences of ~0.01-0.03) are likely not meaningful.

strengths: Addresses a genuine and timely gap: existing LLM memory benchmarks (LoCoMo, DialSim, LongMemEval, etc.) are essentially static reading-comprehension tests, and this paper is among the first to explicitly evaluate procedural memory built from service-time user feedback, with both off-policy and on-policy protocols.

Comprehensive and well-documented framework: 11 public datasets across 3 domains, 4 input/output length formats, 2 languages, with a clear taxonomy (declarative vs. procedural memory; explicit verbose/action vs. implicit feedback) that is a useful conceptual contribution on its own.

Extensive empirical study: 8 baselines (Vanilla, RAG variants, A-Mem, Mem0, MemoryOS, SFT), backbone and user-simulator ablations, noisy-feedback robustness experiments, and detailed efficiency analysis (Figure 4, A.3.8), including the interesting Mem0 pathological slowdown case study in Figure 11.
Good reproducibility posture: anonymous open-source data, simulation scripts, pre-generated feedback logs, baseline implementations, and detailed prompt templates in the appendix.

Honest treatment of negative results: the finding that SOTA memory systems do not beat naive RAG, and are often worse than Vanilla on some task formats, is valuable and well-argued (Section 3.3), with careful analysis of why it diverges from prior work's claims.
weaknesses: The core premise — that simulated feedback constitutes meaningful 'user feedback' — is only moderately supported. The simulator acts as an oracle with access to ground truth and evaluation metadata (A.2.2), so the feedback is closer to distilled judge critiques than realistic user signals; the human annotation study (A.2.5) uses only 200 cases, 9 annotators, and reports very low Fleiss' Kappa (0.093 for naturalness, 0.273–0.380 overall), which is weak evidence and could alternatively be interpreted as annotation ambiguity.

Evaluation methodology is noisy and fragile: LLM-as-judge merging of heterogeneous metrics into a 1–10 score, followed by min-max/z-score aggregation across datasets, can distort conclusions; several per-dataset metrics (e.g., LexEval-Judge ROUGE-L around 0.05–0.14) have very low signal-to-noise, and no statistical significance testing is reported despite small test sets (e.g., 82 cases in HelloBench-A.K.-Writing; DialSim subsets with ~17 evaluated cases, visible as 0.0588=1/17 accuracies).

Coverage is uneven: Mem0 is missing from several cells (Open domain, LiSo) due to excessive runtime, and on-policy results are reported only for a subset of systems and domains, weakening the 'continual learning' claim's evidential basis; the main paper's headline results are off-policy with verbose feedback only.

Originality claim is overstated: the paper asserts it is 'the first benchmark that provides all types of memory and feedback data,' but closely related concurrent work (e.g., MemBench, Tan et al. 2025; MemSim) is cited and dismissed somewhat quickly in Table 1; the differentiation deserves more careful argument.

Some design choices are under-justified: e.g., copy probability fixed at 4× the like probability (Eq. 3), the 600-token long/short threshold, and deterministic satisfaction-score mappings for DialSim/Locomo (S=3/S=9) feel ad hoc; the simulator/backbone coupling (Qwen3-32B simulating feedback for Qwen3-8B systems) may introduce family-specific bias, addressed only via one Mistral ablation.

Presentation issues: Figure 3 is a cluttered radial plot with unreadable small-value labels, Figure 13 references 'Figure .' with a broken cross-reference, and there are recurring grammatical errors and typos (e.g., 'simluation', 'baselinfee', inconsistent 'MemoryBench'/'Memorybench') that suggest a rushed manuscript.
